title: Kejriwal Claims Instagram Account Restricted in India, Demands Explanation From Meta
excerpt: The AAP leader accused Meta of bowing to political pressure after his account was geo-blocked, adding to escalating tensions between the tech giant and Indian politicians.
body:
• Arvind Kejriwal said his Instagram account was restricted in India and demanded Meta explain the action
  • The AAP leader accused Meta of capitulating to political pressure, telling the company to stop "bowing down to PM Modi so much"
  • The incident comes days after Meta's chief global affairs officer apologised to India's IT minister for briefly restricting a post by PM Modi
  • Multiple opposition politicians, journalists, and activists have reported Instagram restrictions during the ongoing student protest movement

Former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal on Wednesday said his Instagram account had been restricted in India, escalating a confrontation between Indian politicians and Meta Platforms over content moderation that has intensified amid the country's largest student-led protests in over a decade.

Kejriwal, the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor, said he had received no explanation from Meta for the restriction. In a pointed message directed at the company, he said Meta should not "bow down to PM Modi so much," framing the action as politically motivated censorship, according to multiple Indian media reports including Hindustan Times and The Hindu.

A Pattern of Restrictions

Kejriwal's complaint follows a cascade of content moderation disputes that have embroiled Meta in India — its largest market by users for both Facebook and Instagram — over the past several weeks.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=YzqdlOnaQjw

On July 28, Facebook briefly restricted a video post by Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressing the student protests that forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Meta said the block was an operational error. India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology subsequently summoned Meta executives to explain, and on August 5, Meta's Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan formally apologised to India's IT minister, according to Reuters.

"I apologised to the minister on behalf of Meta for the error restricting PM Modi's post."

— Joel Kaplan, Meta's Chief Global Affairs Officer

Separately, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg apologised to the Indian government over child sexual abuse material, deepfake content, and other operational lapses on Meta's platforms, financial news publication Moneycontrol reported.

Broader Crackdown on Dissent

The tensions extend well beyond individual politicians. According to MediaNama's censorship tracker, dozens of Instagram accounts belonging to journalists, content creators, and activists have been restricted or had posts removed during the student protests against exam paper leaks. The outlet documented instances of stories, reels, and posts being geo-blocked in India, often with notices citing compliance with government legal requests under India's Information Technology Rules.

Police in Hyderabad registered a case against Meta India head Arun Srinivas over videos posted on Facebook that allegedly depicted Modi in an "abusive manner," Reuters reported on July 31. The case was among several filed by supporters of Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party who alleged that manipulated videos of the prime minister were circulating on Meta-owned platforms.

Meta Caught Between Two Fires

The Kejriwal restriction illustrates Meta's increasingly difficult position in India. The ruling BJP and its supporters have pressed the company to crack down on content they view as disrespectful to the prime minister. Opposition parties and press freedom advocates, meanwhile, accuse Meta of complying too readily with government takedown requests, effectively censoring political dissent.

India's IT ministry in 2023 empowered all federal and state agencies and police to issue content takedown notices for "any information which is prohibited under any law," according to Reuters. In October 2024, the government launched the Sahyog portal to streamline takedown requests — a system that X (formerly Twitter) has challenged in court, calling it a "censorship portal."

Data from Meta shows the company took down three times as much content due to Indian government orders in the first half of 2025 compared to the same period in 2023, The Hindu reported.

What's Next

A Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology, chaired by BJP MP Nishikant Dubey, has been examining Meta's operations in India. With the government simultaneously pressuring Meta to remove anti-Modi content and opposition leaders crying foul over restrictions on their own accounts, the company faces a regulatory landscape with few safe harbours. For NRIs who rely on Instagram and Facebook to follow Indian political discourse, the restrictions are a reminder that what they see from India is increasingly shaped by government takedown orders.
nri_angle: The incident highlights the tightening grip on social media discourse in India, a concern for diaspora users who rely on these platforms to follow Indian politics and connect with audiences back home.
